Gemini-powered speech translation in Google Meet will now support 63 languages across web and mobile devices (Android and iOS), with listening support on Google Meet hardware devices.
Previously, speech translation supported a limited set of language pairs and required configuring a single language pair for the entire meeting. With this update, powered by Gemini 3.5 Live Translate, participants can translate speech between any combination of the 63 supported languages in the same meeting with minimal configuration, helping global and distributed teams collaborate more naturally across language barriers.
We’re changing and simplifying how participants use speech translation during a multilingual call:


Automatic spoken language detection: Meet automatically detects the language being spoken and translates it into each listener's preferred language in near real-time, even when multiple languages are spoken in the same meeting or when a speaker switches languages.
Individual participant controls: Instead of a meeting-wide configuration, participants can independently enable speech translation for themselves using the dedicated translation control in the meeting toolbar, and optionally configure additional languages they already understand so those languages are not translated. 
Synchronized automatically translated captions: When speech translation is active, captions provide a consistent reading and listening experience, matching the translated audio.

# Google Meet Can Now Translate Speech in 63 Languages: What It Means for Your Calls

> **In short:** Google says Meet's speech translation, powered by Gemini, now covers 63 languages. It detects which language is being spoken, so each person in a meeting can hear and read the language they prefer. The announcement did not give a start date.

If you join calls with colleagues, clients, or family in other countries, you have probably had the awkward moment when half the room switches languages mid-sentence. Google's latest update to Google Meet is aimed at exactly that situation.

## What changed

Until now, Meet's speech translation worked with a limited set of language pairs. A language pair is simply two languages translated between each other, such as English and Spanish. Someone also had to choose one pair for the whole meeting before the call started.

Google says the new version is powered by Gemini, the family of AI models behind several Google products. It supports 63 languages, and participants can translate between any combination of them in the same meeting. The company says this is meant to help global and distributed teams talk more naturally across language barriers.

According to the announcement, the update is available on web and mobile, on both Android and iOS, and includes listening support on Google Meet hardware devices.

## How the new pieces fit together

Google points to three changes that matter most in everyday use:

- **Automatic language detection.** Meet works out which language is being spoken and translates it into each listener's preferred language. Google says this also works when several languages are spoken in one meeting, or when a speaker switches languages partway through.
- **Individual choices.** Instead of one setting for everyone, each participant decides whether to use speech translation. You can also list the languages you already understand, so Meet does not translate those for you.
- **Matching captions.** When translation is on, captions follow the translated audio, so what you read and what you hear stay in sync.

Think of it like a personal interpreter who only steps in for the languages you need, rather than one interpreter working for the whole room.

## What this means for you

- **If you run or join a distributed team**: Each person can choose the language they want to hear, which can cut down on "can someone repeat that?" moments. Let your team know the feature exists so they can look for it in their own meetings.
- **If you host client or partner calls**: Automatic detection means you do not have to predict who will speak which language. Still, tell participants in advance which language the meeting will mostly use.
- **If you're just getting started**: Join a Meet call with a colleague who speaks another language and look for the translation option. Test it with a short, simple sentence before you rely on it in an important meeting. If you can't find the option, it may not have reached your account or device yet.
- **If you already use it**: Set the languages you understand, so you hear translation only where you need it. Ask bilingual teammates to check how the captions handle technical terms.

Keep in mind that this article reflects what Google says the feature does. Availability on your account, device, or plan may depend on the rollout, so check Google's Meet help pages for current details.

## Wrap-up

Google says Meet's speech translation now covers 63 languages, detects what is being spoken, and lets each participant decide what they hear and read. For international teams, that could mean fewer language barriers and less guesswork. Your next step: at your next multilingual call, look for the translation option and see how it works for you.
